title: $30 an Hour Is How Much a Year? (2026)
metaDescription: $30/hour is $62,400 a year at 40 hrs/week — $5,200 monthly, $2,400.00 biweekly. See overtime pay tables and a 2026 federal take-home estimate.

hero.lede: Full time at 40 hours a week, 52 weeks a year (2,080 hours). Below: every pay-period equivalent, overtime tables at time-and-a-half, and a 2026 federal-only take-home estimate.

shortAnswer.heading: How much is $30 an hour per year?
shortAnswer.html: $30 an hour is $62,400 a year at 40 hours a week for 52 weeks (2,080 hours). That's $1,200.00 a week, $2,400.00 biweekly, and $5,200.00 a month gross. After estimated federal income tax and FICA, a single filer keeps about $52,318 — and steady overtime at $45.00/hour raises the total fast.

sections.title: What $30/hour adds up to per period.
sections.note: Gross (pre-tax) figures assuming paid hours every week of the year. Unpaid time off reduces them proportionally.

sections.title: $30 an hour in 2026, in plain numbers.
paragraphs: At $30 an hour, a full-time year — 40 hours a week for 52 weeks, with no unpaid time off — grosses $62,400. That's $1,200.00 a week, $2,400.00 per biweekly paycheck, and about $5,200.00 a month before taxes.

Measured against the middle of the U.S. labor market, $30/hour is right around the U.S. median full-time wage — the BLS median works out to about $31.28/hour ($1,251/week, BLS, Q2 2026). The big lever for hourly earners is overtime: every OT hour pays $45.00 at time-and-a-half.

sections.title: Overtime at $45.00/hour changes the math quickly.
sections.note: Overtime rows assume time-and-a-half (1.5 × $30 = $45.00) on hours past 40, every week of the year — the FLSA baseline for non-exempt workers.

sections.title: From $62,400 gross to take-home.
sections.note: Single filer, standard deduction, no state/local income tax, credits, or pre-tax benefits. Actual checks vary.

sections.title: What a single filer actually keeps.
paragraphs: Federally, this wage puts a single filer in the 12% marginal bracket for 2026: $62,400 gross less the $16,100 standard deduction is $46,300 taxable, generating $5,308 of income tax (8.5% effective). Add $4,774 of FICA and estimated take-home is $52,318/year, or $4,359.87/month.

faq.q: How much is $30 an hour per year?
faq.a: $30 an hour is $62,400 a year at full time — 40 hours a week for 52 weeks (2,080 hours). At 30 hours a week it comes to $46,800, and with 10 hours of weekly overtime it reaches about $85,800.

faq.q: How much is $30 an hour biweekly?
faq.a: A standard 80-hour biweekly period at $30/hour grosses $2,400.00. After estimated federal income tax and FICA for a single filer, roughly $2,012.25 remains per check, before state taxes.

faq.q: How much is $30 an hour after taxes?
faq.a: On $62,400 of annual wages, a single filer taking the 2026 standard deduction pays about $5,308 of federal income tax plus $4,774 of FICA, keeping roughly $52,318 a year — about $25.15 per hour worked. State and local taxes reduce this further where they apply.

faq.q: How much is $30 an hour with overtime?
faq.a: Overtime pays time-and-a-half: $45.00 per hour past 40 in a week. A steady 50-hour week earns $1,650.00 weekly — $85,800 a year, $23,400 more than the straight 40-hour year.

faq.q: Is $30 an hour a good wage in 2026?
faq.a: $30/hour annualizes to $62,400, which is right around the U.S. median full-time wage — the BLS median for full-time workers is $1,251/week (about $31.28/hour, BLS, Q2 2026). Local cost of living, benefits, and schedule stability matter as much as the rate itself.

methodology: Annualization is straight arithmetic: $30 × 2,080 hours (40 hours × 52 weeks) = $62,400, with daily/weekly/biweekly/monthly rows derived the same way. No unpaid leave is assumed.
Overtime rows use the FLSA non-exempt baseline of 1.5× base pay ($45.00/hour) on hours over 40 per week, sustained all 52 weeks.
The take-home estimate uses 2026 federal brackets for a single filer with the $16,100 standard deduction plus employee FICA (7.65%). It excludes state/local tax, credits, and pre-tax benefits.
Median-wage comparison: BLS median usual weekly earnings, full-time workers, $1,251/week (BLS, Q2 2026).
